pharm: Topical ascomycin-derivative calcineurin inhibitor that blocks T-lymphocyte activation and inhibits release of inflammatory cytokines, used as a non-steroidal treatment for atopic dermatitis (eczema).
quick: Apply a thin layer of 1% cream to affected skin twice daily; rub in gently
Limited data; minimal systemic absorption - use only if clearly needed
Do not apply to the breast/nipple; minimal systemic absorption otherwise; caution
Skin response, signs of skin infection, lymphadenopathy/skin lesions (malignancy concern)
summary: Pimecrolimus 1% cream is a topical calcineurin inhibitor (a non-steroidal immunomodulator) used as second-line therapy for short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis (eczema) in non-immunocompromised adults and children 2 years and older who have failed, or cannot tolerate, other topical treatments. It is applied as a thin layer twice daily. It works by inhibiting calcineurin in T cells, blocking T-cell activation and the release of inflammatory cytokines that drive eczema. It carries a BOXED WARNING: although a causal relationship has not been established, rare cases of malignancy (skin cancer and lymphoma) have been reported in patients using topical calcineurin inhibitors; therefore long-term continuous use should be avoided, application limited to areas of involvement, and the drug used only as a second-line agent and not in children under 2 years. Patients should minimize sun exposure. Local burning/stinging at the application site is common, especially early. It is not recommended in immunocompromised patients or on skin with active infection.
indications: Second-line therapy for short-term and non-continuous chronic treatment of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis (eczema) in non-immunocompromised adults and children 2 years and older who have failed to respond adequately to, or are intolerant of, other topical treatments

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer of 1% cream to affected skin twice daily and rub in gently and completely
dosage.n: Use short-term/intermittently; stop when eczema clears; reassess if no improvement in ~6 weeks
Use only in patients aged 2 years and older

Wash hands after application unless the hands are being treated; do not apply occlusive dressings
Avoid use on areas of active skin infection; treat infections before/alongside therapy as directed
Limit application to areas of involvement and use for the shortest time needed; avoid continuous long-term use
Minimize natural and artificial sunlight exposure during treatment
moa: Pimecrolimus is a derivative of ascomycin, a natural macrolactam, and belongs to the calcineurin-inhibitor class. It binds with high affinity to the cytosolic immunophilin macrophilin-12 (FKBP-12); the resulting complex inhibits the calcium-dependent phosphatase calcineurin. By blocking calcineurin, it prevents dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT), thereby inhibiting the transcription and synthesis of inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-2, IL-4, IL-10, and interferon-gamma) from activated T cells. It also inhibits the release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells. The net effect is suppression of the T-cell-driven inflammatory cascade that underlies atopic dermatitis, without the skin-atrophy effects associated with topical corticosteroids.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pimecrolimus or any component of the cream
relative: Application to skin with active viral, bacterial, or fungal infection
Netherton syndrome or other conditions with skin-barrier defects (increased systemic absorption); generalized erythroderma
monitor: Skin malignancy and lymphadenopathy (per boxed warning)
Local and systemic infection at treated sites
Treatment response; avoid prolonged continuous use

preg: There are limited human data; systemic absorption after topical application is minimal. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Avoid applying to the breast area if continuing to breastfeed, and follow general precautions for topical immunomodulators.
lact: It is not known whether topically applied pimecrolimus is excreted in human milk; systemic absorption is minimal. Do not apply directly to the breast or nipple area while breastfeeding to avoid infant ingestion, and use with caution elsewhere.
renal: No dose adjustment is necessary; systemic absorption following topical application is minimal, so clinically significant renal elimination is not a consideration.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is necessary because of minimal systemic absorption. Rare reports of systemic effects are not expected at recommended topical use.

major: No clinically significant drug interactions established for topical use (minimal systemic absorption)
moderate: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole, calcium-channel blockers, cimetidine) - theoretical increase in pimecrolimus levels in patients with widespread/erythrodermic disease and greater absorption
minor: Live vaccines - effect during topical use not established; consider in patients with extensive application
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol consumption may cause facial flushing, warmth, or skin irritation (alcohol-intolerance reaction) in some patients during treatment.
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference; routine monitoring focuses on clinical skin assessment.

common: Application-site reactions - burning, stinging, warmth, or soreness (especially early in treatment)
serious: Skin malignancies and lymphoma (rare; causal relationship not established - per boxed warning)
Serious skin infections including eczema herpeticum / disseminated herpes
Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis and angioedema
emergency: Rapidly spreading or systemic skin infection (e.g., eczema herpeticum)

monitoring: Clinical response of eczema; reassess diagnosis if no improvement within ~6 weeks
Signs of local or systemic skin infection at treated sites
Skin examination for new or changing lesions/lymphadenopathy with long-term use (malignancy concern)
Adherence to short-term, intermittent use and avoidance of extensive/continuous application
counsel: Apply a thin layer only to the eczema patches twice a day and rub it in; use it for short periods and stop when your skin clears, as advised
A mild burning or stinging feeling is common when you start and usually improves after a few days
Limit sun and tanning-bed exposure, and use sun protection on treated skin
Do not use on infected skin; tell your doctor if a treated area becomes painful, oozing, crusted, or develops blisters
Drinking alcohol may cause facial flushing or warmth while using this cream; report any new lumps, swollen glands, or skin growths to your doctor
pk: Itch and inflammation improve over days; reassess response at ~6 weeks
Systemic absorption is minimal; blood concentrations are typically very low or undetectable
Systemic half-life not well defined due to minimal absorption (oral data ~30-40 hours)
Symptom control during twice-daily application; used short-term/intermittently
Store at controlled room temperature (do not freeze); keep the tube tightly closed; keep out of reach of children
pearls: BOXED WARNING: rare reports of malignancy (skin cancer and lymphoma) with topical calcineurin inhibitors (causal link not established) - use as SECOND-LINE, short-term/intermittent therapy, apply only to affected skin, avoid continuous long-term use, and do NOT use under 2 years of age
Non-steroidal alternative to topical corticosteroids - useful on the face, eyelids, and skin folds because it does not cause skin atrophy
Local burning/stinging is the most common effect and usually subsides within the first days
Avoid on infected skin and in immunocompromised patients; minimize sun exposure during treatment
Alcohol may trigger facial flushing/warmth; counsel patients accordingly
missed: If a dose is missed, apply it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next application, skip the missed dose and resume the usual twice-daily schedule - do not apply extra cream to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely with topical use because systemic absorption is minimal. If the cream is accidentally ingested, treatment is supportive and symptomatic; contact a poison control center. Excessive topical application is not expected to cause systemic toxicity but may increase local irritation.
